nameStory: The Bronzed Tiger Beetle gets its name from its distinctive metallic bronze coloration that shimmers like polished copper in sunlight. Like other tiger beetles, it earned the "tiger" part of its name from its fierce predatory behavior — these insects are the cheetahs of the beetle world, sprinting after prey with incredible speed and powerful jaws.
description: The Bronzed Tiger Beetle is a small but mighty predator that measures about half an inch long. Its body gleams with a beautiful coppery-bronze sheen, and it has prominent bulging eyes and large, powerful jaws for catching prey. These speedy hunters are often seen darting across sandy or gravelly surfaces on warm days, pausing briefly before zooming off again in pursuit of smaller insects.

idTips.label: Metallic bronze coloration
idTips.description: The body has a distinctive coppery-bronze sheen that catches the light like polished metal, setting it apart from other tiger beetles with different metallic hues

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: About half an inch long with a robust, streamlined body built for speed — feels solid and substantial if you manage to catch one

idTips.label: Hairy thorax
idTips.description: The pronotum (the segment behind the head) is noticeably fuzzy with fine copper-colored hairs that you can see with close observation

idTips.label: Large prominent eyes
idTips.description: Bulging compound eyes that stick out from the head like tiny marbles, giving excellent vision for hunting

idTips.label: Shoulder markings
idTips.description: Look for pale markings on the wing covers where the shoulder marking typically connects to a middle band

idTips.label: Lightning-fast movement
idTips.description: Runs in quick bursts across open ground, stopping abruptly before darting off in another direction — too fast to easily follow with your eyes

habitat: Look for Bronzed Tiger Beetles on sandy beaches, gravel paths, dirt roads, and other open areas with loose soil throughout New England. They particularly favor coastal areas and sandy spots around lakes and rivers where the soil drains well. You'll often spot them in full sun on bare ground where they can easily chase down prey.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active in late spring, emerging to hunt on warm, sunny days. This is prime time to spot them as they're fresh and actively seeking mates.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen hunting during the warmest parts of sunny days. They may become less active during the hottest afternoon hours.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity continues into early fall on warm days, but they become increasingly scarce as temperatures drop and they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Adults are dormant and hidden underground or under debris. The two-year life cycle means larvae are developing in burrows beneath the surface during this time.

funFact: Tiger beetles can run so fast they actually blind themselves — when chasing prey at top speed (about 5 mph, which is incredibly fast for a half-inch insect), they have to stop periodically to let their eyes readjust and relocate their target!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other metallic tiger beetles, but the bronze coloration is distinctive — Six-spotted Tiger Beetles are bright emerald green, while Purple Tiger Beetles have purple or blue-green hues. Remember: "Bronze Tiger = Copper Fire" for the warm metallic color.
compareHints: Among New England's tiger beetles, the Bronzed Tiger Beetle is distinguished by its warm copper-bronze coloration, while the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle shines bright metallic green and the Purple Tiger Beetle displays cooler purple-blue tones. The Bronzed also has more subtle markings compared to the bold white spots of the Six-spotted or the dramatic patterns of the Festive Tiger Beetle.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tiger beetles, the six-spotted stands out for its pure metallic green color - the bronzed tiger beetle has more copper tones, while the festive tiger beetle is darker with different spot patterns.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the festive tiger beetle is distinguished by its particular pattern of white markings and metallic coloration.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Hairy-necked is the only one with those distinctive fuzzy neck hairs.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the twelve-spotted is unique for having exactly twelve spots on a dark body.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Oblique-lined stands out with its exceptionally large compound eyes and distinctive diagonal white markings.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Big Sand Tiger Beetle stands out for its robust, chunky build compared to the more slender Six-spotted or Bronzed Tiger Beetles.
Unlike the bright metallic green Six-spotted Tiger Beetle with its obvious white spots, the Purple Tiger Beetle shows deep purple metallic colors without distinct white markings.

Unlike the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle which prefers woodland paths, or the Bronzed Tiger Beetle found on sandy beaches, the Common Claybank Tiger Beetle is the only New England tiger beetle that specializes in clay habitats.
